summary: Etizolam is a thienodiazepine with pharmacology similar to the benzodiazepines, used short-term for anxiety and insomnia and marketed in countries such as Japan, India, Italy and South Korea. It is NOT FDA-approved in the United States, where it is a scheduled/controlled substance and a recognized drug of abuse. Like benzodiazepines it is habit forming, causes tolerance and dependence, and abrupt withdrawal can precipitate seizures; it carries benzodiazepine-class risks of profound sedation and respiratory depression when combined with opioids or alcohol. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration and taper to discontinue.

Adjunct for anxiety with depressive or somatization symptoms (per Japanese/Italian labeling)

moa: Etizolam is a thienodiazepine in which the benzene ring of classical benzodiazepines is replaced by a thiophene ring fused to a triazole ring. It acts as a positive allosteric modulator at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor-chloride channel complex, enhancing GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission to produce anxiolytic, sedative-hypnotic, muscle-relaxant and anticonvulsant effects. Its active metabolite alpha-hydroxyetizolam contributes to and prolongs the clinical effect.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to etizolam or benzodiazepines
Severe respiratory insufficiency / sleep apnea syndrome
relative: History of substance abuse or addiction
Concomitant opioid or other CNS depressant use
monitor: Respiratory depression, especially with opioids/CNS depressants
Signs of tolerance, dependence, misuse and diversion

preg: Generally classified pregnancy category C with safety not established; benzodiazepine-class agents used late in pregnancy are associated with neonatal sedation, hypotonia and withdrawal. Avoid unless clearly necessary and the potential benefit justifies the risk; weigh maternal benefit against neonatal risk.
lact: It is uncertain whether etizolam is excreted in human milk; as with benzodiazepines, breastfeeding is not recommended. If used, monitor the breastfed infant for sedation, lethargy and poor feeding.
renal: No firmly established dose adjustment; use with caution and consult specialist guidance in significant impairment, monitoring for excess sedation and possible accumulation. Titrate slowly.
hepatic: Metabolized hepatically via CYP3A4 and CYP2C19; use with caution and consider dose reduction in mild-moderate impairment. Contraindicated/avoid in severe liver disease due to impaired clearance and risk of encephalopathy.

major: Opioids - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death (benzodiazepine-class boxed-warning-type risk); avoid or limit dose/duration and monitor
Alcohol and other CNS depressants (sedative-hypnotics, barbiturates, antipsychotics) - additive depression, may be fatal
Strong CYP3A4/CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g., itraconazole, fluvoxamine) - slow elimination and increase etizolam exposure
moderate: CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., carbamazepine) - accelerate metabolism and reduce efficacy
Sedating antihistamines and muscle relaxants - additive sedation
minor: Caffeine may partially antagonize sedative effect
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; avoid large amounts of grapefruit (CYP3A4 inhibition can raise levels).
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; combination causes additive CNS and respiratory depression and may be fatal.
interactions.diagnostics: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers (genetic polymorphism) may have prolonged exposure and exaggerated effects; no major laboratory test interference established.

serious: Physical dependence and withdrawal (including seizures on abrupt stop)
emergency: Fatal overdose when combined with opioids or alcohol

monitoring: Respiratory status if combined with opioids/CNS depressants

Withdrawal reactions during taper or dose reduction

pearls: NOT FDA-approved; this record is SmPC/BNF/Indian formulary-based and pending clinical review - verify against local labeling before use
Habit forming: dependence, tolerance and abuse can occur; abrupt withdrawal can precipitate seizures, so always taper
Carries benzodiazepine-class opioid co-use risk - additive CNS/respiratory depression with opioids or alcohol can be fatal
Active metabolite alpha-hydroxyetizolam (t1/2 ~8.2 h) outlasts the parent drug and prolongs clinical effect
Metabolized by CYP3A4/CYP2C19; CYP2C19 poor metabolizers and CYP inhibitors can markedly prolong effects
Scheduled/controlled in many jurisdictions (e.g., US Schedule I temporary, UK Class C, UN Schedule IV) and a recognized drug of abuse
Flumazenil can reverse overdose sedation but may precipitate seizures/withdrawal in dependent patients
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next scheduled dose, in which case skip it and resume the regular schedule. Do not double up. For bedtime insomnia dosing, skip the missed dose if it is no longer near bedtime. Because etizolam is habit forming, do not change the dosing schedule without medical advice.
overdose: Overdose causes CNS depression ranging from drowsiness, confusion, slurred speech, ataxia and diminished reflexes to hypotension, respiratory depression and coma; effects are markedly worsened and may be fatal when combined with opioids, alcohol or other CNS depressants. Provide supportive care with airway and ventilatory support and IV fluids; consider activated charcoal if early and airway protected. Flumazenil may reverse sedation but can precipitate seizures and withdrawal in chronic/dependent users and is not first-line. Contact a poison control center.
